chunks: From him, from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from al-Muhsin ibn Ahmad, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The moon was eclipsed, so my father went out and I went out with him to the Sacred Mosque, and he prayed eight rak'at, just as one prays one rak'ah with two prostrations.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What we act upon is what we have previously stated, that the prayer of the eclipse is ten rak'at and four prostrations, according to the details we have clarified. The reason for these two narrations being different is taqiyyah (dissimulation), because they are consistent with the opinion of some of the Sunnis. And that which confirms what we have stated is what was narrated:

key_terms.الْعَامَّةُ: The general public (often referring to Sunnis in this context)

ai.seo_question: How many rak'at are in the lunar eclipse prayer according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the jurisprudential nuance between Imam al-Sadiq’s eight-rak'ah prayer during a lunar eclipse and the established Shia practice of ten rak'at with four prostrations. The author attributes the discrepancy to *al-taqiyyah* (dissimulation), noting that the shorter prayer aligned with the Sunni majority view to avoid confusion or persecution. This underscores the Shia method of reconciling conflicting reports by prioritizing the more detailed and robustly supported legal ruling.
